17.0.3.en: Job reached a bitter state, and he counted himself as one dead. In the previous passage he looked at his remaining life as a short journey, a few years and then he would pass from this world without return. Here, in the midst of his bitterness, he counted that his spirit had become corrupt, that the light of his life had been extinguished, and that, while on the dunghill, he had become like one who dwells in the graves.

17.0.4.en: He did not say, "Surely the grave is mine," but "the graves." It is as though the graves of his fathers, which received them, were preparing to receive him also. The graves open their doors to snatch up humanity, and it is fitting for the believer, for his part, to prepare to enter as a victor and conqueror.

17.0.5.en: * No one can go from here to there as long as God has not called him. If God is the One who bound soul and body together, man does not loose them so that they may be joined in a new way. The soul does not separate itself from the body. Job said this, not because the common enemy was threatening him with death, but because he had been struck with his sickness. This is the reason for his asking in his prayer to leave the world.

17.0.6.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * The spirit is crushed by fear of the judgment. The more the chosen feel the final judgment drawing near, the more they are terrified in their minds with fear, as they discover themselves. When they find in themselves any carnal thought, their souls are crushed by the zeal of their repentance... They judge themselves and discipline themselves more strictly, for they await the stern Judge coming at the doors. Therefore they always look to their departure as near.

17.0.7.en: But as for the minds of the lost, they suppose that they will live here for a long time, and so they practice many evil things.

17.0.8.en: Therefore the spirit of the righteous is crushed, and the spirit of the wicked grows fat...

17.0.9.en: ["My days are shortened, and the grave alone is left for me."] For he who contemplates what he will be in death is always in fear, because from now on he lives as one who lives according to what he sees, indeed truly lives as in the eyes of his Creator...

17.0.10.en: Perfect life is attained by thinking of death, where the righteous man strives to escape from the snares of sin. Therefore it is written: ["Whatsoever thou takest in hand, remember the end, and thou shalt never do amiss"] (Sir 7:40).

17.0.12.en: One of the chief exercises in the life of the Desert Fathers, as in the life of those who are earnest about their salvation, is remembering the hour of death, or the last day of the Lord's coming, not out of fear of judgment, but in preparation to enjoy the eternal glories, and for deliverance from the fate of the wicked.

17.0.13.en: * When you approach your bed, say to it: "This very night perhaps you will be my grave, O bed, for I do not know whether this night, instead of my temporary sleep, I shall have the permanent sleep."

17.0.14.en: So, while you have two feet, hasten to work, before you are bound with that chain which, once placed, is never loosed again.

17.0.15.en: While you have two hands, stretch them toward heaven in prayer, before the arms fall from their joints, so that when you desire to draw them back you will not be able.

17.0.16.en: While you have fingers, sign yourself with the cross, before death comes, which looses the proper strength of their nerves.

17.0.17.en: While you have two eyes, fill them with tears, before the hour comes when dust covers your black garments, and your eyes are fixed in one direction with a gaze that you neither grasp nor know. No, rather fill your eyes with tears while your heart is governed by the power of discernment, before your soul is shaken by its departure from it, and leaves the heart a house abandoned by its dweller.

17.0.18.en: O wise man, do not be deceived by expecting a long life!

17.0.19.en: * When the merchant finishes his work he hurries to his house. As long as the monk (the person) has not yet completed his part in the righteous struggle, he feels bitterness when he thinks of his departure from his body. But when he perceives in himself that he has redeemed the time (Eph 5:16) and has received his earnest, he desires to see the life to come. The merchant at sea fears inwardly lest the waves rise against him and scatter the hope of his work. So the monk (the person), as long as he is in this world, is governed by fear lest a sudden storm arise against him and shatter the work in which he has striven from his youth to old age. The merchant fixes his eye on the shore, and the monk (the person) fixes his eye on the hour of his death.

17.0.20.en: St. Isaac the Syrian * There was a brother who was fervent in prayer, and while his brother was performing the service, tears overcame him and at times he forgot passages of the Psalm. The brother begged him one day to tell him what he was thinking about during the service that made him weep so bitterly. He said to him: "Forgive me, my brother, for I always meditate during the service on the Judge, and my standing before Him, for I am a guilty criminal under interrogation. And since I find no justification for myself, I stand terrified, and my mouth is shut, and a verse of the Psalm slips past me. Forgive me for troubling you; let us each perform the service alone." The brother answered: "No, father, for I live without compunction, and at least when I see you I am ashamed." And when God saw his humility, He granted him the compunction that his brother had. Let us also keep our eyes on this gift, so that we may have the same benefit as this brother.

17.0.21.en: From the sayings of the Desert Fathers

17.1.s.en: 2. A cry for help from the Lord

17.1.0.en: 2 "Are there not mockers with me? and doth not mine eye continue in their provocation? 3 Lay down now, put me in a surety with thee; who is he that will strike hands with me? 4 For thou hast hid their heart from understanding: therefore shalt thou not exalt them. 5 He that delivers his friends to plunder, even the eyes of his children shall fail. 6 He hath made me a byword of the peoples, and I have become one to be spit upon in the face. 7 Mine eye also is dim by reason of sorrow, and all my members are as a shadow.

17.1.1.en: "Are there not mockers with me? and doth not mine eye continue in their provocation?" [2].

17.1.2.en: While Job sees the graves preparing to receive him, he sees around him his friends as deceivers, mocking him and insulting him to his face. They turned the sittings into quarrels instead of consolations. His saying "continue in their provocation" reveals that they spent the whole day with him in quarrels, so that even when they left him at the end of the day, nothing stayed in his mind all night but these quarrels that accompanied him.

17.1.3.en: The text here is translated from the Hebrew, differing from that in the Septuagint and also in the Vulgate. In the Septuagint translation it reads: "In distress I make supplication: what shall I do? Strangers steal my goods."

17.1.4.en: Anxiety besieged Job's soul, for he saw the battle raging. He stands, not before his friends, who had become strangers to him, bearing a spirit of enmity against him without cause, but he sees behind them the enemy of good, the devil, with all his forces resisting him. These are the strangers to the human race, who have no work but to rob man of the divine blessings he enjoys and the heavenly glories prepared for him. They are adversaries of mankind, desiring to humble it so that it may share their eternal fate in hell!

17.1.5.en: * Why (was he in distress)? Because Job asks in his prayers that death may come. He is like one defending himself, since he is troubled by the trials, for he does not fully know what is the secret of his trials which the enemy pours upon him. For this reason he says: "What shall I do?"

17.1.6.en: There follows: ["Strangers steal my goods"] (see Job 17:2) LXX. Job calls the demons strangers because they are deceivers, and enemies because they are by nature truly strangers to our race. As for the stealing of his goods, he said this not because they robbed Job of his goods, but because they lied against God like one who steals words, when the slanderer, their chief, said to God: ["But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face"] (see Job 1:11)... But as for God, since He knows the theft (committed by the accuser) by his words, He permitted him the trial in order to prepare Job for the shining sign of victory. For truly, as a conqueror, he dares to say: "Who is this? Let him join hands with me" [3 LXX].

17.1.7.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * ["I have not sinned, and my eye dwells in bitterness."] It is as though he expresses himself in plain words: "I have committed no sin, and yet I bear stripes." But with regard to this point, we consider that in many passages Job confesses that he is a sinner and that his mind moves with thought, so why does he deny here that he committed sin? He gives us the reason himself quickly. He has not sinned to the degree that makes him deserving of the blows of the rod, and he is not able to be without sin.

17.1.8.en: For he was struck not to be corrected from sin, but to enjoy more grace. The Judge Himself bears witness, He who praises even while He strikes.

17.1.9.en: But I think we understand these words better if we understand them of our Redeemer, for He did not sin and at the same time "undertook bitterness"; being without sin, He undertook the punishment of our sin.

17.1.11.en: Origen sees that the saints also have their personal sins. And Ernest Latko says: [In his comment on the term "saints" as applied to the people of God, Origen reminds us in one of his Homilies on the book of Numbers that their being saints does not mean that they are exempt from committing sin. Their holiness is not absolute but relative, consisting in the consecration of their lives to the Lord, who by His goodness preserves them from the graver errors.]

17.1.12.en: * Those who are not saints die in their sins, but the saints repent of them. They bear their wounds and recognize their faults. Then they go to the priest seeking healing, or they seek cleansing through the bishop.

17.1.13.en: * ["Be holy, for I am holy, says the Lord"] (Lev 7:20). What does He mean by saying, "for I am holy"? That is, as I withdraw and keep far from everything that is worshiped, whether on earth or in heaven, and as I am exalted above every creature, and withdraw from what my hands have made, so also you should reject everything that is not holy or consecrated to God...

17.1.14.en: And finally, this word, which is called hagios in Greek Αγίου, indicates something far removed from the earth.

17.1.15.en: * But if you wish to remember other saints, the words of the Holy Bible will answer you: "For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not" (Eccl 7:20). Christ alone has "two perfect hands," "who did no sin" (1 Pet 2:22), that is, His hands have works perfect and complete.

17.1.16.en: Origen We can say that Job did not commit a sin unto death, but as he himself confesses, he is not a man without sin, even if his life were but one day.

17.2.0.en: "Who is he that will strike hands with me?" [3]

17.2.1.en: Although Job says that he did not commit a sin deserving all these blows, he confesses that he is indebted to God and needs a surety or guarantor able to take his place, to stop the seizure and to deposit the bond.

17.2.2.en: The Holy Bible has often referred to the role of the surety or guarantor: ["A good man will be surety for his neighbour: and he that is impudent will forsake him. Forget not the kindness of thy surety, for he hath given his life for thee"] (Sir 29:19-20).

17.2.3.en: Job found no man on earth, not even among his dearest friends, to testify to his innocence, and no one standing on his side as a surety or guarantor, but all turned into adversaries to him. Hence he found no one to turn to but God Himself, who knows the secrets of his heart, his intentions, and his hidden and open conduct.

17.2.4.en: In the name of all humanity he cries out to God, asking Him to be a surety for him. For there is none who can pay our debt and represent us before the divine Presence but the divine Word incarnate, and as St. Augustine repeats in his address to God, saying that there is no refuge to flee to from God except to take refuge in God Himself.

17.2.5.en: * He (the Lord Christ), who did not sin in thought or in deed, became in bitterness through His sufferings. He was freed by the Resurrection, and by His Ascension came to be beside the Father, where He ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of God (to be surety for us).

17.2.7.en: * Before the coming of our Lord and Savior, all the demons reigned over the minds and bodies of men and settled in their spirits. Then the grace of the Lord the Savior appeared, and His mercy on earth, teaching us how the soul of every man ought to regain its freedom and recover the image of God in which it was created...

17.2.8.en: Who is this, if not Jesus Christ, who by His stripes healed us who believe in Him, when He [spoiled principalities and powers] who were among us and "made a shew of them openly" upon the Cross? (Col 2:15).

17.2.9.en: * We fell under the authority of our enemies, that is, "the prince of this world" and his helpers from the powers of evil. Hence arose our need of redemption by Him who buys us so that we may return from the state of estrangement from Him, and so our Savior gave His blood as a ransom for us...

17.2.10.en: And since "the forgiveness of sins," which follows redemption, is impossible before man is set free, we must first be freed from the authority of him who took us captive and kept us under his control, freed beyond the reach of his hand, so that we may be able to obtain the forgiveness of our sins and healing from the wounds of sin, so that we may accomplish works of godliness and other virtues.

17.2.11.en: * "We have peace with God" (Rom 5:1), through our Lord Jesus Christ who reconciled us to God through the sacrifice of His blood... Christ came to destroy the enemies and to make peace, and to reconcile us to God, from whom the barrier of evil that we raised by our sins had separated us.

17.2.12.en: Origen "For thou hast hid their heart from understanding."

17.3.0.en: "Therefore shalt thou not exalt them" (glorify them) [4].

17.3.1.en: As for his friends, because of their ill intent the Lord took away from them wisdom and discernment. The wisdom that was given them by God departed from them, for He took it back, because they did not deserve it. For where there is no compassion toward the suffering, God takes away understanding from their hearts, honor leaves them and shame clings to them, and they come to be in a state of collapse, not in growth and elevation. Consequently they have no ability to perceive God's mercy, nor the discernment to understand His dealings, especially when He permits affliction for His believers.

17.3.2.en: * It is beneficial for us that our enemies be limited in wisdom and stripped of it. For this reason Paul says: ["But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory: which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory"] (1 Cor 2:7-8).

17.3.3.en: ["Therefore shalt thou not exalt them"]... Why? For what is to our benefit, so the knowledge of the truth is hidden from them (the demons); and since they desire evil, they wish to make us ignorant and to blaspheme the Creator.

17.3.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem The text in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) reads, "Thou hast removed their hearts from discipline," and in the Septuagint translation: "Thou hast removed their heart from wisdom." So when God took away from Job's friends understanding or wisdom, He took away from them the knowledge of God's wisdom regarding discipline, for He disciplines with afflictions to build up and approve, and not to tear down and destroy!

17.3.5.en: Those who receive divine discipline with understanding and discernment have their hearts crushed with repentance, and enjoy glory. "For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not?" (Heb 12:6-7).

17.3.6.en: * Rejoice while you are under the stripes, for the inheritance is kept for you, because He does not cast off His people. He disciplines for a time, and does not condemn forever.

17.3.7.en: St. Augustine * ["Thou hast removed their hearts far from discipline"] [4]. For if they had recognized the aim of discipline, and had never despised the commandments of our Redeemer, the very condition of their mortal body (which is under discipline) would have stirred them toward the love of immortal life...

17.3.8.en: Now some bear stripes but do not shape their lives to be renewed by the fear of the Lord who scourges them. Therefore it was rightly said now: ["Thou hast removed their hearts far from discipline."] That is, although the body is under discipline, the heart is not under discipline as long as the person struck with the rod has not returned to humility of mind. He did not say this as if the Almighty, the merciful God, had removed man's heart far from discipline. Rather, after man's fall by his own will, God permits him to remain in his state of fall...

17.3.9.en: ["Therefore they are not exalted"]; for if the heart is under discipline, it seeks the things above, and does not open its mouth to ask for temporal things... Whereas those who give themselves up to base pleasures long always for the goods of the earth. They will not lift up their hearts toward the delights of heaven; for if they lifted up their minds toward hope in the heavenly city, they would be glorified...

17.4.0.en: "He that delivers his friends to plunder, even the eyes of his children shall fail" [5].

17.4.1.en: The matter does not stop at depriving these deceivers of understanding or of the inward insight to know God's wisdom, but they also harm their offspring, since they see in their fathers that they dealt wrongly with their friends.

17.4.2.en: The text in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) reads: "The devil promises his friends plunder, and the eyes of his children fail." It is as though Job compares the children of God with the children of the devil. The former fall under discipline for their exaltation, their glory and their eternal inheritance, while to the latter the devil gives false promises of obtaining spoils, which are temporary, passing gifts, while they perish eternally.

17.4.3.en: Pope Gregory sees that before he spoke of the wicked in the plural, and now he speaks of their head, the devil, in the singular. As the head, he can at times direct the speech in the name of the wicked, and at times in the name of their father the devil. For what belongs to the head belongs to the whole body, and what belongs to the body is also attributed to the head. He also says that the devil, the chief of all the wicked, makes promises to his friends the demons and evil spirits, that he will give them spoil which is nothing but the sons of men who have become captives to him!

17.4.4.en: * "He (the devil) promises his friends spoil, and the eyes of his children fail." After the blessed Job uttered a statement concerning the company of the wicked, that is, concerning the body of the ancient enemy, he passes at once to a statement concerning their leader himself (the devil), the head of all the children of perdition. He passes from the plural to the singular, because Satan and all the wicked people are one body. It often happens that the body takes the name of the head, and the head is given the title of the body...

17.4.5.en: The head takes the title of the body, as was said of the fallen angel himself: "An enemy hath done this" (Mt 13:28).

17.4.6.en: The chief of all the wicked has some as companions, and some as sons. Who are his companions but the fallen angels who fell with him from the throne of the heavenly city? And who are the others who are his sons but the wicked men, who are born through his evil urging to practice evil? So also it was said by the voice of Truth to the unbelievers: "Ye are of your father the devil" (Jn 8:44).

17.4.7.en: This wicked one is the source of error; he promises spoil to his companions, as he promises the evil spirits the souls of wicked men, which they hold to the end.

17.4.8.en: "And the eyes of his children fail," for he sets earthly things as a goal before men to look to, and makes them love what they cannot keep for long. For the tendency of a love wrongly directed cannot endure when it is shown that both the lovers and the things loved quickly become nothing at all.

17.5.0.en: "He hath made me a byword of the peoples, and I have become one to be spit upon in the face" [6].

17.5.1.en: His friends, who used to desire to sit with him, and sought his favor and praised him, came to mock him in his affliction, and to count him an example and a lesson to every hypocrite and wicked man, that no one may imitate him.

17.5.2.en: Job became a living image of those who live in the Lord, whom the world mocks, and, if possible, spits in their face. He was also a type of the Lord Christ, whom the wicked mocked, so that He became a laughingstock, and they spat in His face.

17.5.3.en: "Our soul is exceedingly filled with the scorning of those that are at ease, and with the contempt of the proud" (Ps 123:4).

17.5.4.en: "I was a derision to all my people; and their song all the day" (Lam 3:14).

17.5.5.en: "I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting" (Isa 50:6).

17.5.6.en: "Then did they spit in his face, and buffeted him; and others smote him with the palms of their hands" (Mt 26:67).

17.5.7.en: "And they spit upon him, and took the reed, and smote him on the head" (Mt 27:30).

17.5.8.en: "And some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to buffet him, and to say unto him, Prophesy: and the servants did strike him with the palms of their hands" (Mk 14:65).

17.5.9.en: "And they smote him on the head with a reed, and did spit upon him, and bowing their knees worshipped him" (Mk 15:19).

17.5.10.en: "And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment" (Heb 11:36).

17.5.11.en: * "We are exceedingly filled with contempt" (Ps 123:3). All who wish to live godly in Christ must endure insult (2 Tim 3:12). It is fitting that they be despised by those who do not choose to live in godliness. They despise those who seek the happiness that cannot be seen with their eyes, and they say to them: "What do you believe, you madman? Has anyone returned from the lower world and given you a report of what happens there? Look, I see and enjoy what I love; you are despised, because you hope for what you do not see."

17.5.12.en: "Our soul is exceedingly filled with the scorning of those that are at ease (the rich), and with the contempt of the proud" (Ps 123:4). We ask: who are the rich? He explained this by saying "the proud." Scorning and contempt are one, as the rich and the proud are one. Why are the rich proud? Because they want to be happy here... Perhaps they mock when they are happy, boasting in the arrogance of their wealth. When they are puffed up with their condition, filled with conceit because of their vain honor, they mock us. It is as though one says: Look, it is better for me to enjoy the good things before me. Let those who promise what they cannot show keep away from me. What I see I hold; what I see I enjoy, that I may walk prosperously in this life, so that you may be in greater safety, because Christ is risen and you have learned that He will give you another life, so be assured that He will give it to you.

17.5.13.en: St. Augustine * The Lord of majesty humbled Himself and was rejected by all... He heard mockery on every side, from the Pharisees and from every human being. It is grievous to the heart to look at how they spat in His face, crowned Him with a crown of thorns, and struck His cheeks, as it is written: "I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting" (Isa 50:6). Now if God was willing to humble Himself, and to bear such sufferings, insults and shame, do not think about how far you humble yourself, you whose nature is of the mire, subject to death, and there is no comparison between you and your Lord in this matter. You are proud and puffed up. And God came and took your burden to give you His rest, and you do not wish to bear toils and sufferings; by your toils your wounds are healed.

17.6.0.en: St. Macarius of Alexandria "Mine eye also is dim by reason of sorrow, and all my members are as a shadow" [7].

17.6.1.en: Job became a man of sorrows and tears, until his eyes grew dim. Grief so intensified in him that it wore away his flesh, and he became like a skeleton, or like a shadow, with nothing in him but skin and bones.

17.6.2.en: Job portrays to us his bitter condition: from the intensity of grief his eyes grew dim, or became darkened, unable to see the light of divine truth. Truth had almost disappeared. His friends had turned into enemies resisting him with all their might, supported in this by their resources. And what befell Job himself justifies their conduct, he who had almost become like a shadow without substance. Everything was taken from him, and without cause!

17.6.3.en: On the other hand, it portrays to us the condition of the believer or the Church, not only during the suffering of the bitter troubles from the wicked, but the intense grief that comes upon the believer or the Church as a whole for every soul that turns aside from the way of truth and strays from true knowledge. For this the Apostle Paul cries out, saying: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?" (2 Cor 11:29).

17.6.4.en: These feelings are lived by men of God, whether in the Old or the New Testament, who, having experienced the sweetness of communion with God, cannot bear that anyone be deprived of it.

17.6.5.en: The psalmist says: ["Dejection has overcome me because of the sinners who forsake Your law"] (Ps 119:53). And Jeremiah the prophet says: "Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!" (Jer 9:1).

17.6.6.en: * ["My eye is dim with indignation, and all my members are as though they had become nothing"] [7]. The eye becomes dim with indignation when those very persons are granted the light of truth... and see themselves despised for a long time, and made light of by the wicked. They are bewildered in amazement at the shameful judgment, and fail to fathom the mystery of God: why are the wicked permitted to prevail over the innocence of the righteous? Who is not astonished when he sees Herodias, by her daughter's dance, receive from the hand of the drunken king the head of "the friend of the bridegroom," the prophet, and more than a prophet, presented before the faces of his guests on a platter (Mt 14:6-11; Lk 7:26)?

17.6.8.en: * If the righteous see a person among the sons of the Law transgress it, they are grieved and saddened, because the pain of one member makes all the members suffer.

17.6.9.en: Anthimus, Bishop of Jerusalem * Among sinners there are those who sin without the Law (Rom 2:12), because they did not know the Law. And others sin in the Law, because by transgressing it they hold it in contempt. "Dejection has overcome me because of the sinners who have cast away Your law" (Ps 119:53). Truly, if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it (1 Cor 12:26). So it is fitting for us to suffer for our sinful brethren because they sin, and to take the same attitude as this saint (the psalmist).

17.6.10.en: St. Didymus the Blind * He who sheds hot tears over the faults of his neighbor is healed by his sorrow for his brother.

17.6.11.en: St. Basil the Great * Let us weep for them, not one day or two, but all the days of our life.

17.6.12.en: St. John Chrysostom * Ah, beloved ones! If we are to obtain consolation from sorrows, rest from toils, health from diseases, and immortality after death, it is not right for us to grieve over the sicknesses that befall mankind, nor to be anxious because of the trials that come upon us.

17.6.13.en: We must not fear if those who fight against Christ (the Arians) plot against the righteous; rather we please God the more because of these things, as we are made readier and trained in the life of virtue. For how shall we obtain patience unless there are troubles and sorrows?

17.6.14.en: And how can nobility be shown except by our enduring mockery and injustice?

17.6.15.en: And how can endurance be tested unless there is an attack from enemies (the Arians and others)?

17.6.16.en: And how can our longsuffering be proved if there are no slanders from those who are against Christ (the Arians)?!

17.6.17.en: And finally, how can man perceive virtue unless the evils of the wicked first appear?!

17.6.18.en: So our Lord went before us in this when He wished to show men how to endure... When He was struck, He bore it patiently, and when He was reviled, He reviled not again, and when He suffered, He threatened not, but gave His back to the smiters, and His cheeks to those who struck Him, and turned not His face from spitting (1 Pet 2:23; Isa 50:6).

17.6.19.en: And finally it was His will to be led to death so that we might see in Him the image of all virtues and of immortality, and so walk following in the steps of His footprints, and truly tread upon serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy (sin).

17.6.20.en: St. Athanasius the Apostolic * Let us think of the captivity of our brethren as our own captivity. The sorrow of those in danger is our own sorrow. You must be sure that there is one body. Not only love but also godliness urges and encourages us to save the members of our family.

17.6.21.en: St. Cyprian the Martyr * Paul does not mean that he pretends to be weak with them, but that he sympathizes with their weakness.

17.6.22.en: St. Augustine * What wondrous tenderness in the shepherd (Paul)! Others fall, and he says, affirming his grief over the stumbling of others, that it kindles the fire of his pains. May all those to whom the care of the rational flock is entrusted imitate him, and prove that they are no less than the shepherd who for many years tends an irrational flock. This does not happen even if some neglect occurs, but in our case, if one sheep is lost or falls prey, the loss is enormous, and the harm and the terror and the punishment are unspeakable. Above all this, if our Lord accepted the shedding of His blood for its sake, what excuse justifies him who allows himself to neglect one who has value in the Lord's sight, and does not exert every effort on his part to care for him?

17.7.0.en: 8 Upright men shall be astonied at this, and the innocent shall stir up himself against the hypocrite. 9 The righteous also shall hold on his way, and he that hath clean hands shall be stronger and stronger.

17.7.1.en: "Upright men shall be astonied at this, and the innocent shall stir up himself (rise) against the hypocrite" [8].

17.7.2.en: When the righteous hear what befell Job of successive afflictions, and of his friends' attitude toward him, they stand in amazement, wondering. They think that God has left the earth and abandoned His believers, so the innocent rises against the hypocrite, that is, he cannot bear this, and seeks out this providence of God which seems obscure. The innocent rises to stand against the ungodly, defending the truth or rejecting every false interpretation.

17.7.3.en: * ["The righteous are astonished at this, and the innocent is stirred up against the hypocrite"] [8]. The "innocent" in this place is understood as the righteous man who is not yet perfect, who is beginning in good ways. For although he does not think of harming others, he is not able to practice perfect things. When the hearts of the little ones see the wicked flourishing in the present life, they burn with the coals of envy... Now the innocent is inflamed against the hypocrite, since he is not accustomed to harm anyone but envies the glory of the hypocrite.

17.7.4.en: But if the innocent in this passage means one who is perfect in his goodness, ["the innocent is moved against the hypocrite"] when he sees him thriving and scorns him and his thriving. Then he preaches the true things, and says that he must be despised by others whenever they see in him a longing for things that he cannot keep for long.

17.7.6.en: * "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity. For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb" (Ps 37:1-2). What seems to you a long time is "soon" in God's sight. When you submit yourself to God, the long time becomes "soon" for you also... You make things trifling and worthless, appearing only on the surface of the earth, with no roots in the depths. In winter they are green, but when the summer sun scorches them they wither. Now it is winter; your glory is not as it appears outwardly, but if your love has a deep root like many trees in the winter, the frost will go and summer will come (the day of judgment); then the greenness of the grass will wither and the glory of the trees will appear.

17.7.7.en: * I observed the wicked, and I saw them in peace, but what peace? A temporary peace, changing, passing and earthly, and yet I too ask this from God. I saw those who did not serve God receiving what I desired, I who serve God, but my feet were slipping and my steps had slid (Ps 73:2). Now I understood why they have peace and thriving on earth... because their punishment is not temporary, but fixed forever.

17.8.0.en: St. Augustine "The righteous also shall hold on his way, and he that hath clean hands shall be stronger and stronger" [9].

17.8.1.en: When the righteous man sees the wicked prospering while trials and afflictions come upon the righteous and the just, the righteous man does not withdraw from the way of fellowship with God, but grows more steadfast in his resolve and advances holding the more firmly to his way. He sees that the troubles that befall the righteous turn to their growth and their enjoyment of greater strength.

17.8.2.en: The spiritual man experiences the earnest of heavenly life, so he is not shaken before the temporary success of the wicked, nor troubled before trials and afflictions. He finds his happiness in perseverance in the Spirit of the Lord, who gives surpassing sweetness to fellowship with the Lord Christ in His cross, and always kindles the depths of the believer toward seeking heavenly things, despising every temporal gift.

17.8.3.en: The true believer does not cease to persevere against sin and in enjoying the holy life, because of his enjoyment of fellowship with the Lord.

17.8.4.en: * The hypocrite obtains the things of this world by an evil will. But the righteous man is bound and fettered more strongly by the love of heavenly things.

17.8.6.en: * If we keep the rule of perseverance and practice discernment with knowledge, where the fruit of life is harvested, then the struggle is with the attacks of passions that are in no way able to approach our mind.

17.8.7.en: St. Isaac the Syrian * We to whom eternal life has been given do good works, not for the sake of reward, but to preserve the purity that has been given us.

17.8.8.en: St. Mark the Ascetic * It is very beneficial to read the Holy Bible, for it makes the soul wise, directs the spirit toward heaven, moves man to thanksgiving, destroys the desire for earthly things, and lets our minds continually contemplate the world to come.

17.8.9.en: St. John Chrysostom * ["(The judgments of the Lord) are sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb"] (Ps 19:10). As the soul is bound to become pure honey, freed from the bonds of mortal life, it awaits in simplicity the blessings of the divine banquet; or it is in the honeycomb, wrapped in this life as in the cells of the wax, which it fills without becoming like them (that is, without becoming wax). And in this it needs the help of God's hand, which presses not to crush, but to make it drip honey. The judgments of the Lord become for such a soul sweeter than its own being, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

17.8.10.en: St. Augustine * Consider the Orthodox manner in the battle and appreciate the achievements of spiritual battles, how the Christian combatant, having conquered his rebellious body and put it under the weight of his feet, is carried forward as a victor on high. Therefore he does not run as uncertainly, because he trusts that he will enter at once into the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem.

17.9.0.en: 10 "But as for you all, do ye return, and come now: for I cannot find one wise man among you. 11 My days are past, my purposes are broken off, even the thoughts of my heart. 12 They change the night into day: the light is near to the darkness. 13 If I wait, the grave is mine house: I have made my bed in the darkness. 14 I have said to the grave, Thou art my father: to the worm, Thou art my mother, and my sister. 15 And where is now my hope? as for my hope, who shall see it? 16 They shall go down to the bars of the pit, when our rest together is in the dust."

17.9.1.en: "But as for you all, do ye return, and come now: for I cannot find one wise man among you" [10].

17.9.2.en: Job demands that they turn back from what they are thinking, and realize that there is not one wise man among them, because they ask him to repent so that prosperity and the comfort of the world may return to him, thinking that in this is the consolation of the suffering. They are not wise, because they have turned their eyes from the consolations of heaven to the comfort of the world. The happiness of the righteous is in their hope in eternity, not in their obtaining a temporal good.

17.9.3.en: It is as though he tells them that it would be foolish for him to listen to them and answer their requests, and so grant them what is temporal.

17.9.4.en: * "Well, come now, rise up all of you, for I do not find truth in you" (Job 17:10) LXX. It is as though he says: Come, and you who are cooperating together, enter into a heated debate against me.

17.9.5.en: Job knows that one alone pursues a thousand, and two can put ten thousand to flight (Deut 32:32). There is no need of a great number of combatants, especially when they are armed with falsehood.

17.9.6.en: I see decisively that there is no truth in you; therefore I surely urge you all to the battle.

17.9.7.en: One must marvel at the bold spirit in Job's words. For after his friends trampled him underfoot, so that we cannot imagine how he suffered, yet he did not cease to contend with them, nor did he abandon his patience, which made him fearsome to his enemies.

17.9.8.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem The text in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) reads: ["But as for you all, change your way and come now"] [10]. It is as though Job answers them by saying: If you ask me to repent of sins I have not committed, you fall into the sin of slander and unjust accusation. I advise you to turn back from this way of yours, and your evil conduct, then you may come to me, and we can come to an understanding together.

17.9.9.en: The Pope sees here that Job calls them to two works: the first negative, which is to cease from sin, and the second positive, which is doing good. This is what he meant by their changing their evil way and coming to him bearing good works.

17.9.10.en: * Paul asks us to be dead to the world, for this death is beneficial to us, being the beginning of a new life. So also he commands us to be fools to the world, that by this we may enter into true wisdom. You become fools to this world when you despise earthly wisdom, and trust that it contributes nothing to our understanding of the faith.

17.9.11.en: St. John Chrysostom * The wisdom of this world is that which lacks the grace of God; it is wholly human in its characteristics.

17.9.12.en: Theodoret * They must change their way, and come. The change is by faith, and the coming by practice; or they must change by leaving evil works, and come by practicing good works. As it is written: ["Depart from evil, and do good"] (Ps 37:27).

17.9.13.en: ["Perhaps I shall not find one wise man among you"] [10]. What does it mean that he exhorts them to wisdom, and at the same time longs not to find them wise, except that they cannot come to true wisdom when they are deceived by their trust in their own vain wisdom?

17.9.14.en: It is written of this: "Be not wise in thine own eyes"(a) (see Isa 5:21). It was also said: "Be not wise in your own conceits" (Rom 12:16).

17.9.15.en: In this the great preacher (Paul) gives counsel to those whom he found carnally wise, that in order to obtain true wisdom they must first become fools, saying: "If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise" (1 Cor 3:18). And the Truth Himself says: "I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes" (Mt 11:25). So, because those who are wise in their own eyes cannot come to true wisdom, the blessed Job, longing for the change of his hearers, truly desired that [no wise man be found among them]. It is as though he says plainly: "Learn to be fools in yourselves, that you may be truly wise in God."

17.9.17.en: * Do not let abundance of wisdom become a stumbling block to your soul, and a snare in your path; rather, firm trust in God makes for you the beginning of the way filled with blood (the way of spiritual striving against sin), lest you be found continually in want and bare of the knowledge of God, for the fearful man who watches the wind never sows.

17.9.18.en: St. Isaac the Syrian "My days are past."

17.10.0.en: "My purposes are broken off, even the thoughts of my heart" [11].

17.10.1.en: They ask Job to repent of his evil and hypocrisy so that what he lost may return to him. As for him, these matters have no place in his heart. His days have passed or are hastening to the end, and the former purposes of his heart, works of reform and care for the poor, have been taken from him. Job has come to see death not far from him, so he does not think about what he cannot do.

17.10.2.en: Pope Gregory sees that Job is a symbol of the persecuted Church. When tribulation greatly intensifies upon her, her thought rises all the more toward heaven, so she is not occupied with earthly matters, not even with purely social service, but is confined to eternal glory. And what we say of the Church as a holy company is fulfilled in the life of each member in her, when he meets affliction with thought of heavenly things.

17.10.3.en: * ["My days pass away, my thoughts are scattered, they pain my heart"] [11]. The holy Church sees that the periods of her life pass in periods of day and night, for when she is in distress she has night, and when she is in prosperity she has day. For the light dawns in the calm of peace. At times she listens to the service of temporal matters... So also the blessed Job, whether by his own voice or by the voice of the universal Church, after experiencing that his days had passed, went on: ["My thoughts are scattered, they pain my heart."] When temporary glory departs from the minds of the righteous, even obligations to earthly matters are taken away from them... At times in their earthly obligations they are bound to descend to thinking of lower things, and feel within themselves that they are in torment. And it also happens that the very hostile work of persecution turns for them into great rejoicing because of the rest of heart they obtain.
